title: The Hosting Decision That Determines Whether a Client Ever Calls You Angry
title_hi: The Hosting Decision That Determines Whether a Client Ever Calls You Angry
summary: I run a small WordPress studio — webmaster.co.ua, 18 years, 235+ projects. If I had to isolate the single decision that
content:
I run a small WordPress studio — webmaster.co.ua, 18 years, 235+ projects. If I had to isolate the single decision that predicts how many angry calls I get post-launch, it's not the code, the design, or the CMS. It's which hosting plan the client picked.

Cheap shared hosting generates support tickets that look like your fault. A site that's technically well-built on a $3/month shared plan still goes down during traffic spikes, still runs slow on shared CPU, still gets flagged when a neighboring site on the same server gets blacklisted. None of that is your code failing. All of it reads to the client as "the website you built is broken."

Clients choose hosting on price, because nobody explains what the price is trading away. Left alone, most small-business clients pick the cheapest hosting option, because from their side, hosting is an undifferentiated commodity line item. It isn't — it's the difference between a site that survives a local news mention and one that falls over from it. Explaining this once at project start costs five minutes and prevents most of the "your website is down" calls that come six months later.

We stopped treating hosting recommendation as optional. It's not in most contracts, and it's easy to let clients self-select their host to keep the sales conversation simple. But vetting hosting has quietly become part of the actual deliverable for us, even when it's not billed as one — because an outage on bad hosting damages the same trust that a bug in our own code would.

The client's mental model is "is the website working," not "whose responsibility is this." When something breaks, they don't parse out hosting versus code versus DNS versus their own domain renewal lapsing. They just know something they paid for stopped working. Being the person who explains and fixes it — regardless of whose layer it's actually in — is what keeps the retainer, technically at fault or not.

If you build sites and hand off hosting decisions entirely to clients, it's worth revisiting — the support burden that follows is often a hosting problem wearing a "the website is broken" costume.

content:
Gamify Your GitHub Profile: Levels, XP and Streaks as Live SVG Cards


Your GitHub profile README is one of the first things people see when they land on your account. It is a small piece of real estate where a lot of developers now showcase who they are — and, increasingly, what they have been building.

One of the most popular ways to fill it is with dynamically generated stats cards. The community has built some wonderful tools around this idea, and they have made countless profiles look great. Still, most of them share a similar shape: counters, bars and numbers in a fixed layout.

I wanted to try a different angle: what if your GitHub activity felt more like a game?

That is how I ended up building gh-stats-xcards — a self-hostable service that renders your GitHub data as gamified SVG cards, with levels, XP ranks, streaks and contribution charts. Everything you need to make your profile stand out, embedded with a single line of Markdown.




  
  
  The core idea: your contributions are XP


Instead of showing a plain total, the level card treats your all-time contribution count as experience points:

[
\text{level} = \left\lfloor \sqrt{\frac{\text{XP}}{\text{base}}} \right\rfloor + 1
]

The base value defaults to 100 and can be tuned via an environment variable (LEVEL_BASE_XP), so the curve can be as generous or as steep as you like.

As your level grows, so does your rank title: Bronze → Silver → Gold → Platinum → Diamond → Legend.

The card also shows your total contributions, contributions in the current year, and a progress bar toward the next level. It is a small thing, but it adds a fun "what level am I at?" moment every time you check your own profile — and it gives visitors an at-a-glance sense of how active you are.

  
  
  The card lineup


There are eight card types, each designed for a different spot in your README:

  
  
  Level & alternate layout


The main card above, plus a level-alternate variant with a different arrangement of the same data — useful if you want two complementary cards side by side.

  
  
  Profile card (vertical)


A compact vertical card with your avatar, contribution stats, PR and issue totals, and your top public repositories ranked by stars:



  
  
  Profile footer (wide)


A wide horizontal card that fits nicely at the bottom of a README. It shows your top three repositories in a single line plus a level ring:



  
  
  Contribution graph


A line/area chart of your recent contribution activity, so visitors can see the rhythm of your work at a glance:



  
  
  Streak


A three-column card showing your total contributions since your first contribution day, your current streak (with a ring, a fire icon and a small pop-in animation), and your longest streak:



  
  
  Top languages


A donut chart of the primary languages across your public repositories — a compact way to show your tech stack:



  
  
  Embedding is one line


Once you have your username and a deployment URL, adding a card to your profile README is as simple as:



[![GitHub Stats xCards](https://gh-stats-xcards.fly.dev/stats/YOUR_USERNAME?card=level&theme=dark)](https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME)






For HTML or other contexts, you can use the image URL directly:



<img src="https://gh-stats-xcards.fly.dev/stats/YOUR_USERNAME?card=github&theme=tokyonight&show_avatar=true" alt="GitHub stats" />







  
  
  Themes and colors


Cards ship with a catalog of built-in themes — dark, tokyonight, radical, dracula, vision-friendly-dark, pastel, minimalist, vue and more. If none of them matches your README's look, every card also accepts per-token hex overrides:




Parameter
What it controls




bg_color
Card background


title_color
Title and headings


text_color
Body text


icon_color
Icons and accents


border_color
Border and dividers


accent_color
Progress bars, highlights, chart accents




So you can match any theme you are already using, down to the exact hex value.


  
  
  A few technical details worth mentioning


Since the cards are rendered server-side, there is a bit of engineering behind them that I enjoyed putting together:



Stack: FastAPI + Jinja2 templates + the GitHub GraphQL API. The SVG templates are plain Jinja files, which makes adding a new card type straightforward.

Caching: Successful responses are cached for six hours by default (Cache-Control: public, max-age=21600), with an X-Cache-Hit header so you can inspect what is happening. You can disable it while iterating on templates.

Avatars without the blocklist: with show_avatar=true, the profile photo is embedded into the SVG as a data URI, so GitHub does not block the external avatar URL when the image is loaded from a README.

Rate limits: for production traffic the service recommends a GitHub personal access token — and since the project is self-hostable, you can run your own instance with your own token and never share limits with anyone.



  
  
  Run your own instance


Self-hosting is one of the core goals of the project. The requirements are modest: Python 3.12 and an optional GitHub token.



python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_xxxxxxxx   # recommended for production traffic
uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000






Or use the included Docker image:



docker build -t gh-stats-xcards .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 -e GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_xxxxxxxx gh-stats-xcards






The repo includes configuration examples for Fly.io, Render and Vercel, plus a small interactive preview UI at the root URL and Swagger docs at /docs.


  
  
  Give it a try


The live instance is free to use — try it with your own username:


Level card: https://gh-stats-xcards.fly.dev/stats/YOUR_USERNAME?card=level&theme=dark

Streak card: https://gh-stats-xcards.fly.dev/stats/YOUR_USERNAME?card=streak&theme=tokyonight

Contribution graph: https://gh-stats-xcards.fly.dev/stats/YOUR_USERNAME?card=contribution-graph&theme=dracula



The project is MIT licensed and open source: github.com/LuiisDev21/gh-stats-xcards. If you build a card layout you love, or find a metric you wish existed, contributions and ideas are very welcome.

Happy leveling! 🎮

content:
How I Cut LLM Token Usage by Up to 60% in Production

If you work with LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), you know the pain: every call costs money, and a big chunk of that cost is pure waste — verbose prompts, code pasted with no filtering, repeated context the model doesn't even need to understand the task.

That's why I built PromptShrink: a prompt pre-processor that trims the excess before it ever hits the API, without losing what actually matters for the model to understand.

The real problem

Every time you feed a code snippet or a long prompt to an LLM, you're paying per token, not per character. Comments, whitespace, formatting meant for humans — all of that is dead weight the model doesn't need to do its job. At scale (thousands of calls per month), that adds up to a real bill.

What PromptShrink does
Packages entire repositories, minifying code and stripping comments, ready to paste as context into any LLM
Simulates real dollar savings, comparing your current spend against the optimized version
Visualizes everything on a dashboard — tokens saved, % reduction, active rules
Plugs straight into your code via a Python SDK
Becomes a browser extension, adding a "Shrink" button directly on ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Google AI Studio, and Poe
In practice
bash


  
  
  Package an entire project into optimized context


promptshrink repo --path ./src --save-to-file context.txt


  
  
  Simulate monthly savings


promptshrink calc --calls 100000 --tokens 800 --model gpt-4o

Running calc on a scenario of [insert your real number here, e.g. "100k calls/month with gpt-4o"], the estimated savings came out to [$X per month] — just by trimming what's unnecessary before it reaches the model.

Try it out

The project is open source, with a CLI, a FastAPI backend, and a Python SDK. If you're running LLMs in production and want to stop paying for tokens that add zero value, check it out:

🔗 github.com/HeloisaPeGarcia/PromptShrink

Feedback and PRs are very welcome — this is my first published project like this, so every contribution helps make it better.
